Lessons.Title: Compare and Order Fractions
ExplanationParagraphs: Learning goal: Compare and order fractions using an efficient, accurate strategy. Different fractions may be compared using benchmarks, equal numerators/denominators, equivalent fractions, or common denominators.
Original 2021 source warm-up (10 min): 5×6, 5×12, 6×12, and 11×12. Explain how knowing one product helps you find another.

Original source Activity 1 Compare Fractions Game (20 min): groups 2–4 use the Grade4 fraction-card deck. The greater (or greatest) fraction wins the round; equal greatest fractions trigger another draw among tied players. Keep track of difficult comparisons and justify the winners.

Original source Activity 2 Fractions in Order (15 min): Order each of the four sets below from least to greatest. Start with two sets independently, then discuss with a partner. Show mathematical reasons rather than copying the answer.
Use a common whole. Benchmark fractions against 1/2 or 1, convert when needed, and carefully handle close values like 101/100 versus 21/20.
Teacher-led lesson synthesis (10 min): discuss multiple ordering methods, defend your reasoning, and identify two specific skills learned in this unit.
Edulytics independently authored Cool-down, NOT the publisher's gated original: arrange 3/8, 1/2, 2/3 from least to greatest and explain. Open explanation requires teacher review.

KeyConcepts.Title: Flexible comparisons
KeyConcepts.Definition: Fractions may be compared by benchmarks or exact equivalence.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Check common whole, then use a mathematically valid strategy.

KeyConcepts.Title: Increasing order
KeyConcepts.Definition: Ascending order means every adjacent fraction is no larger than the next.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Compare exact rational values; group by 1/2 and 1 to reduce work.

KeyConcepts.Title: Equivalent fractions and ties
KeyConcepts.Definition: Different representations can have exactly the same value.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Equal values trigger another card in the source game.

WorkedExamples.Title: Benchmark then order
WorkedExamples.Question: Order 1/4, 3/4, 2/3 from least to greatest.
WorkedExamples.Method: Place 1/4 below 1/2, then compare 2/3 and 3/4 by twelfths.
Steps: 1/4 is less than both other fractions.

WorkedExamples.Title: Equivalent fraction tie
WorkedExamples.Question: Which card wins: 3/6 or 2/4?
Steps: These cards are equivalent, so follow the source tie rule.

WorkedExamples.Title: Independent exact fraction reasoning
WorkedExamples.Question: Which is larger: 7/12 or 2/3?
WorkedExamples.Method: Convert to equivalent equal-sized fractional parts and check the comparison.
WorkedExamples.Check: First-party mathematical calculation; original pupil diagrams and open reasoning require separate teacher review.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Picking the larger printed denominator as the larger number.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: A denominator alone describes part size, not whole value.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Compare equivalent forms or benchmark relationships.
Use exact rational comparisons, e.g. 101×20 versus 21×100.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Forgetting ties in the card game.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Different names can show equal rational values.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Check equivalence and replay the tied round according to source rules.

SummaryPoints: Source: 10-minute Number Talk, 20-minute Compare Fractions game, 15-minute ordering, and teacher synthesis.
The four original ordering problem sets are presented without the four finished answer keys in learner content.
Exact numeric pair and three-fraction ordering Practice is reused, while four-item source reasoning stays teacher assessed.
